docs.title: What this documentation assumes
docs.text:
That you will read the code when the answer really matters. Every page here was written against the implementation, and where the behaviour is surprising that is stated on the page rather than hidden. When this site and the code disagree, the code is right — and the page has a defect, which is worth reporting.

Every page can be taken with you

The Download .md button hands you the original Markdown file, exactly as it sits in the repository. Save as PDF opens the browser print dialog with a stylesheet that strips the navigation — what comes out is the content alone. Both sit in the top bar of every page, next to the font selector, and the whole documentation exists in Portuguese and English.

docs.title: API overview
docs.text: fast-param-manager is the product's server: a FastAPI application over MongoDB, with authentication delegated to Keycloak and end-to-end OpenTelemetry instrumentation.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text: Does Does not Stores parameters grouped by application Notify anyone when a value changes Validates the value against its declared type Coerce types automatically Encrypts secret, user and users Keep a history of values Authorizes writes by role Protect reads by default Emits spans and metrics for every operation Negotiate client versions

docs.title: Public surface
docs.text:
Three route groups, with different access regimes:

Prefix Purpose Who gets in /auth Token issue and refresh, user info Open to issue, authenticated for userinfo /parameters The application and parameter CRUD Varies per route — see Endpoints /admin Runtime configuration Admin only

The route-by-route detail, with request and response bodies, is in Endpoints.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
An application is a document; the parameters are a map inside it. Each parameter carries the value plus the metadata that governs validation:

{
  "value": "postgres://...",
  "description": "Connection string for the reporting database",
  "type": "secret",
  "user_editable": false,
  "min_length": 0,
  "max_length": 30,
  "min_value": 0,
  "max_value": 1000000,
  "referenced_params": null
}

The bound defaults are surprising

max_length defaults to 30 and min_value defaults to 0. That means a 40-character string is rejected and a negative number is rejected — in both cases without anyone having configured anything. The bounds are detailed in Parameter types.

On read, each parameter comes back enriched with audit metadata: created_at, created_by, updated_at and updated_by.

docs.title: How a request crosses the API
docs.text:
The server is strictly layered, and one rule holds everything together: the controller never touches the database.

flowchart TD
    accTitle: Path of a request through the API
    accDescr: The request enters through the middleware that validates the Keycloak token, goes down through controllers, services and repositories, and ends at MongoDB. Keycloak, crypto_utils and OpenTelemetry sit alongside, wired to the layer that uses them.

    C["HTTP client<br/>param-manager · curl · frontend"]

    subgraph server["fast-param-manager"]
        direction TB
        M["middlewares/keycloak_auth<br/>validates RS256 JWT via PyJWKClient<br/>get_current_user · require_admin"]
        K["controllers/ — FastAPI routers<br/>wiring by Depends<br/>get_read_user resolves READ_AUTH_MODE<br/>off · warn · enforce"]
        S["services/ — business rules<br/>AppService · RuntimeConfigService<br/>_validate_permission · _encrypt_value"]
        R["repositories/ — Mongo access<br/>AppRepository · RuntimeConfigRepository<br/>compare-and-swap on params_version"]
    end

    D[("MongoDB<br/>singleton opened and closed by the lifespan")]
    KC["Keycloak — external<br/>issues and signs the token<br/>/auth/token · /refresh · /userinfo"]
    CR["security/crypto_utils<br/>PBKDF2 100k + AES-GCM<br/>salt · master_key · crypto_data"]
    OT["OpenTelemetry<br/>a span per operation<br/>+ metrics"]

    C --> M
    M --> K
    K --> S
    S --> R
    R --> D

    M -. JWKS .-> KC
    S -. secret/user/users .-> CR
    K -. span .-> OT
    S -. span .-> OT
    R -. span .-> OT

Each layer owns something the others are not licensed to take over: every business rule lives in services/, every data access in repositories/, and the controller merely translates HTTP into a business call. The per-layer detail, including the test contract that Depends injection creates, is in Architecture.

The access gate for each route — read, token or admin — is in the Endpoints table.

docs.title: Versions that disagree
docs.text:
An honest warning for anyone about to package or release: there are currently three version declarations that contradict each other in the server repository.

Where Value pyproject.toml 0.1.0 CHANGELOG.md 2.0.0 API_VERSION and service.version in traces 2.0.0

On top of that, CHANGELOG.md was hand-written in a format that does not match the configured title_format, and towncrier has never run on this project. Running towncrier build without resolving that first produces a corrupted changelog.

docs.title: How the token is validated
docs.text:
Identity comes from Keycloak. The middlewares/keycloak_auth.py middleware validates the JWT with PyJWKClient and algorithms=['RS256'] — that is, it fetches the realm's public key and verifies the signature. The server issues no token of its own; it only checks what Keycloak signed.

Three dependencies come out of that, and the names matter because the test suite overrides them one by one:

get_current_user Requires a valid token. Fails with 401 if there is none. get_current_user_optional Resolves the user if a token is present; returns None instead of failing. require_admin Requires a valid token and the admin role.

docs.title: The roles
docs.text:
There are two, and the difference between them is narrow and precise:

admin Can do everything: create and delete applications, create and delete parameters, change any field of any parameter, and change runtime configuration. user Can change only the value field of parameters flagged user_editable=True. Anything else is 403.

What enforces this is AppService._validate_permission, which diffs the restricted metadata fields. The question it answers is not "did the user touch the value?" but "did the user touch anything beyond the value?".

docs.title: READ_AUTH_MODE
docs.text:
Out of the box, reading a parameter is anonymous. That is not an oversight: it is the historical behaviour, and the server does not negotiate client versions — tightening the control overnight would take down every fleet member that does not yet send a token.

The mode is resolved by RuntimeConfigService, which gives precedence to the value stored in the database (changeable by an admin without a redeploy) and falls back to .env when there is no override.

Mode What it does off Historical behaviour. Anonymous reads allowed, with no resolution cost warn Still allows them, but counts and logs every read without a token enforce Requires a token. Without one, 401

docs.title: The promotion criterion
docs.text:
warn exists to produce a measurement, not to warn a person. It feeds the anonymous-read metric.

Only promote to enforce with the metric at zero

While anonymous_reads_total is not zero in the environment, there is a consumer without a token — and turning enforce on will take it down.

docs.title: An invalid token does not count as an anonymous read
docs.text:
A subtlety that looks like a detail and is not. Under warn, a request arriving with an Authorization header that does not resolve — expired token, wrong audience — is recorded as an authentication failure, not as an anonymous read.

If the two were counted together, a fleet with a momentarily expired token would keep the anonymous counter above zero forever, and the gate could never be promoted. The very signal that decides promotion would be corrupted by noise.

docs.title: USER_EDITABLE_ENFORCEMENT
docs.text:
The same two-stage switch pattern, applied to write authorization.

legacy (default) The diff is computed against the whole payload, with schema defaults filled in. Consequence: a plain user gets 403 even when editing a user_editable parameter, because the defaults enter the diff as if they were deliberate changes. explicit The diff considers only the fields the client actually sent, and preserves already stored metadata. This is the behaviour you want.

Promotion depends on adoption of client 0.4.3, which started omitting user_editable from the payload when the caller does not supply it. Version 0.4.2 sends user_editable=False explicitly — under explicit, that becomes an attempt to change metadata and goes back to 403.

docs.title: Authentication routes
docs.text:
Route Body Returns POST /auth/token username and password as form fields The Keycloak token POST /auth/refresh refresh_token as a form field A refreshed token GET /auth/userinfo — (token in the header) Data about the authenticated user

The first two use application/x-www-form-urlencoded, not JSON.

docs.title: What is frozen in the OpenAPI document
docs.text: tests/test_openapi_contrato.py freezes securitySchemes and the per-route security block. It is what turns "the published schema did not change" from an argument into a check. Do not delete that test when touching authentication dependencies — it is the only automated barrier that exists in this area.

docs.title: A secret that reaches the history
docs.text:
Deleting the file does not delete the commit

A Keycloak client_secret, a database password or an encrypted envelope that lands in a commit stays reachable by anyone holding the repository, even after the file disappears from the working tree. git log keeps the content, not the final state.

What ends the exposure is rotating the secret at its source — in Keycloak, in the database, wherever it is issued. Rewriting history does not replace that: in an already distributed repository, filter-repo invalidates every clone and recovers nothing that has already been read.

That is why the pipeline's secret scan runs over the whole history, not over the commit diff: what is already in has to be found where it is.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All server configuration goes through a single object: Settings, in core/config.py, instantiated once at module level.

Never call os.getenv in server code

If the variable is not in Settings, it does not exist for the application. Reading the environment directly bypasses validation and creates invisible configuration.

Loading uses env_file='.env', case_sensitive=True and extra='allow'. case_sensitive means mongo_host is not read in place of MONGO_HOST.

docs.title: MongoDB
docs.text:
Variable Default MONGO_HOST localhost MONGO_PORT 27017 MONGO_USER admin MONGO_PASSWORD admin MONGO_DATABASE fast_param_manager MONGO_AUTH_SOURCE admin

Access goes through a classmethod singleton in core/database.py, opened and closed by the FastAPI lifespan.

docs.title: Keycloak
docs.text: Variable Default KEYCLOAK_URL http://localhost:8081 KEYCLOAK_REALM fast-param-manager KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID fast-param-api KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET (none)

docs.title: READ_AUTH_MODE
docs.text:
Defaults to off. Accepts off, warn and enforce, in increasing order of strictness — the order is what lets you tell whether a change loosens or tightens the control.

An invalid value here kills the application at boot, on purpose: the .env is controlled at deploy time, and a typo must surface immediately instead of silently becoming anonymous reads in production. The value coming from the database takes another path — it arrives at runtime and is coerced with an error log, without bringing anything down.

Details and the promotion criterion are in Authentication and authorization.

docs.title: USER_EDITABLE_ENFORCEMENT
docs.text:
Defaults to legacy. Decides how the restricted-field diff is computed on upsert.

legacy Compares against the whole payload, with schema defaults filled in. This is the historical behaviour: a plain user always gets 403, even on a parameter flagged as editable. explicit Compares only the fields the client actually sent, and preserves already stored metadata.

Do not promote early

explicit is only safe once param-manager 0.4.3 has been adopted. Version 0.4.2 sends user_editable=False explicitly, and under explicit that starts counting as an attempt to change metadata.

docs.title: Application and cryptography
docs.text: Variable Default Note APP_CUSTODY_KEY dev-chave-custodia-app Change it in production. It is the root of secret custody SECRET_KEY your-secret-key-here ALGORITHM HS256 ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES 30

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS is a comma-separated list; the default is *.

* turns credentials off automatically

* with allow_credentials=True is an invalid combination per spec and browsers reject it. While the list is *, credentials are disabled. For cookies and Authorization to work in the browser again, fill it with the real domains: https://front.example.com,https://admin.example.com.

docs.title: API identity
docs.text: Variable Default API_TITLE Fast Param Manager API API_VERSION 2.0.0 API_DESCRIPTION API para gerenciamento de parâmetros com MongoDB e Keycloak

docs.title: OpenTelemetry
docs.text:
Variable Default OTEL_SERVICE_NAME fast-param-manager OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT otel-collector:4317 OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL grpc OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_INSECURE true OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER / OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER otlp OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL 10000 OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES service.version=2.0.0,deployment.environment=dev OTEL_PYTHON_LOG_CORRELATION true OTEL_PYTHON_LOGGING_AUTO_INSTRUMENTATION_ENABLED true OTEL_PYTHON_LOG_LEVEL debug OTEL_PROPAGATORS tracecontext,baggage COLLECTOR_OTLP_ENABLED true

See Observability.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Eleven routes in three groups. The Access column uses three values:

read Resolved by get_read_user — depends on READ_AUTH_MODE. Anonymous under off and warn, requires a token under enforce. token Requires a valid token of any role. admin Requires the admin role.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Method Route Access Success POST /auth/token open 200 POST /auth/refresh open 200 GET /auth/userinfo token 200 POST /parameters/apps/ admin 201 GET /parameters/apps/ read 200 DELETE /parameters/apps/{app_name} admin 200 PUT /parameters/apps/{app_name}/params/ token 200 GET /parameters/apps/{app_name}/params/ read 200 GET /parameters/apps/{app_name}/params/{param_name} read 200 DELETE /parameters/apps/{app_name}/params/{param_name} admin 200 GET /admin/read-auth-mode admin 200 PUT /admin/read-auth-mode admin 200

POST /parameters/apps/ returns 201, and it alone

Everything else returns 200. The client compares the status exactly, so this asymmetry is part of the contract — see Compatibility.

docs.title: POST /auth/token
docs.text:
Form body, not JSON:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/auth/token \
  -d "username=my-user" \
  -d "password=my-password"

docs.title: POST /parameters/apps/ — create an application
docs.text:
Access admin. Success 201.

{
  "name": "MY_APP",
  "description": "My application for doing..."
}

Response:

{ "message": "...", "app": "MY_APP" }

docs.title: GET /parameters/apps/ — list applications
docs.text:
Access read.

{
  "apps": [
    {
      "name": "MY_APP",
      "description": "...",
      "total": 12,
      "created_at": "2026-01-15T10:30:00",
      "created_by": "matheus",
      "status": true
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: DELETE /parameters/apps/{app_name} — delete an application
docs.text: Access admin. Returns { "message": "..." }.

docs.title: PUT /parameters/apps/{app_name}/params/ — write parameters
docs.text:
Access token — but what a plain user can actually change depends on user_editable and on USER_EDITABLE_ENFORCEMENT.

The body is a map from name to parameter, which lets you write several in a single request:

{
  "TIMEOUT_HTTP": {
    "value": 30,
    "type": "int",
    "description": "Timeout for outbound calls, in seconds",
    "max_value": 300
  },
  "DB_PASSWORD": {
    "value": "r3al-p4ssw0rd",
    "type": "secret"
  }
}

The response is the state after the write, with audit metadata:

{
  "app": "MY_APP",
  "params": {
    "TIMEOUT_HTTP": {
      "value": 30,
      "type": "int",
      "description": "...",
      "user_editable": false,
      "min_length": 0,
      "max_length": 30,
      "min_value": 0,
      "max_value": 300,
      "referenced_params": null,
      "created_at": "2026-01-15T10:30:00",
      "created_by": "matheus",
      "updated_at": null,
      "updated_by": null
    }
  }
}

A secret comes back encrypted

A secret, user or users parameter comes back as an envelope, never in the clear. The client is what decrypts it. See Cryptographic envelope.

docs.title: GET /parameters/apps/{app_name}/params/ — read all
docs.text: Access read. Same ParamsResponse shape as above.

docs.title: GET /parameters/apps/{app_name}/params/{param_name} — read one
docs.text:
Access read.

{
  "param": {
    "value": 30,
    "type": "int",
    "created_at": "2026-01-15T10:30:00",
    "created_by": "matheus",
    "updated_at": null,
    "updated_by": null
  }
}

Note the wrapper is {"param": {...}} — one level more than seems necessary. That is contract: the client unwraps exactly that shape.

docs.title: DELETE /parameters/apps/{app_name}/params/{param_name} — delete one
docs.text: Access admin. Returns { "message": "..." }.

docs.title: GET /admin/read-auth-mode
docs.text:
Access admin. Shows the current mode and where it came from:

{
  "mode": "warn",
  "source": "database",
  "env_default": "off",
  "updated_at": "2026-02-01T09:00:00",
  "updated_by": "matheus",
  "previous_mode": "off"
}

source is only ever env or database. When it is database, a stored override is winning over .env.

docs.title: PUT /admin/read-auth-mode
docs.text:
Access admin. Body:

{ "mode": "enforce" }

mode is restricted to off, warn or enforce; any other value is rejected by the schema. The response has the same shape as the GET, with previous_mode filled in.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer to run locally
  • Docker and Docker Compose for the full stack
  • A reachable MongoDB
  • A Keycloak, if you are going to exercise authentication

docs.title: Local environment
docs.text:
cd fast-param-manager
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
Copy-Item .env.example .env

PowerShell is not bash

The project README carries bash commands (cp, source venv/bin/activate) that need translating. And PowerShell 5.1 has no && — chain with cmd1; if ($?) { cmd2 }.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
task run INFO: Started server process INFO: Waiting for application startup. INFO: Application startup complete. INFO: Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8001 (Press CTRL+C to quit)

Which is shorthand for:

opentelemetry-instrument uvicorn fast_param_manager.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8001

Without the wrapper, the application runs blind

Running uvicorn directly works — but without opentelemetry-instrument there are no traces, no metrics and no log correlation. The symptom is subtle: the API responds normally and the dashboard stays empty.

docs.title: Full stack with Docker
docs.text:
The compose files live in docker/, not at the project root as the README suggests:

File Contents docker/docker-compose.yaml The whole stack docker/api/, docker/keycloak/, docker/mongodb/ Per-service splits docker/observability/, docker/dockge/ Observability and container dashboard docker/etc/ Configuration for prometheus, loki, tempo, promtail, otel-collector and grafana

.env must exist before you bring it up.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text: Service Port API (docker) 8000 API (task run) 8001 nginx 8080 Keycloak 8081 Mongo Express 8082 Grafana 3000 MongoDB 27017 OTLP 4317 / 4318

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
pyproject.toml declares Poetry, but requirements.txt is the source of truth for versions — everything pinned with ==.

PyJWT needs the crypto extra

The middleware validates tokens with PyJWKClient and algorithms=['RS256'], which requires cryptography. That used to arrive transitively through python-jose; once python-jose was removed, the extra became mandatory. Forgetting it fails only in production, because the test suite mocks Keycloak.

Another trap in the same file: uvloop needs a platform marker (; sys_platform != "win32"). The freeze is produced in a Linux container but the same file is installed on the Windows development machine, where the package does not build.

docs.title: Requirements file encoding
docs.text: The files are UTF-8 without a BOM. When regenerating, do not use pip freeze > file nor Out-File -Encoding utf8 (which writes a BOM on PowerShell 5.1). Use [System.IO.File]::WriteAllLines with UTF8Encoding($false), or generate inside a container and copy.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
task test                      # lint, then pytest with coverage
pytest . -m "not integracao"   # unit only
pytest . -m integracao -v      # only what talks to a real resource

The integration suite needs a reachable MongoDB. Outside CI it skips itself — meaning task test without Mongo proves nothing about integration:

docker run -d --name mongo-teste -p 27019:27017 `
  -e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME=admin -e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD=admin123 mongo:7

Then set MONGO_HOST, MONGO_PORT, MONGO_USER, MONGO_PASSWORD and MONGO_AUTH_SOURCE.

Teardown noise, not failure

Pymongo's background monitor logs after pytest closes its streams and prints a ValueError: I/O operation on closed file at the end of the run. Read pytest's summary line, not the trailing traceback.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: The API is instrumented with OpenTelemetry end to end: traces, metrics and correlated logs, exported over OTLP to a collector.

docs.title: The wrapper is not optional
docs.text:
opentelemetry-instrument uvicorn fast_param_manager.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8001

Without opentelemetry-instrument the application starts and responds normally — and emits nothing. The symptom is an empty dashboard next to a healthy API, which is a particularly nasty thing to diagnose because nothing is broken.

docs.title: The instrumentation pattern
docs.text:
Every controller, service and repository module declares, at the top:

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

And every operation follows the same shape:

with tracer.start_as_current_span('operation_name') as span:
    span.set_attribute('operation', 'operation_name')
    span.set_attribute('app.name', app_name)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    ...
    record_db_query_duration(time.perf_counter() - start, {...})
    span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.OK))

A new endpoint replicates that. It is not decoration: it is what makes a trace cross all three layers instead of showing only the HTTP edge.

docs.title: Metrics and the dashboard
docs.text:
Metrics are consumed by docker/etc/grafana/dashboards/fast-param-manager-dashboard.json.

A metric label is contract

The dashboard matches on labels. Renaming or repurposing a metric breaks the dashboard silently — it still loads, with an empty chart. Check the dashboard JSON before touching any metric name, and treat this as part of the contract described in Compatibility.

Two metrics deserve a mention because they exist to support a decision, not to fill a panel:

anonymous_reads_total Reads without a token, counted while READ_AUTH_MODE is warn. It is the number that authorizes — or forbids — promotion to enforce. authentication failures Counted separately from anonymous reads. A request with a token that does not resolve lands here, not in the anonymous counter. Mixing the two would corrupt the promotion signal.

docs.title: Log correlation
docs.text: With OTEL_PYTHON_LOG_CORRELATION on, log records carry the current span's trace_id. In practice: given a slow trace in Tempo, you can jump straight to that request's log lines in Loki, without hunting by timestamp.

docs.title: Local stack
docs.text:
The observability stack comes up alongside everything else in docker/:

Component Role Port otel-collector Receives OTLP and fans out 4317 / 4318 Tempo Traces 3200 Loki Logs 3100 Prometheus Metrics — Promtail Container log collection — Grafana Visualization 3000

Configuration lives in docker/etc/.

docs.title: In the tests
docs.text:
Spans are asserted with InMemorySpanExporter, through the otel_memory_exporter fixture. An autouse fixture called clear_spans resets the exporter between tests — without it, one test would see the previous test's spans.

Which means the instrumentation pattern is testable and is tested: a new endpoint that forgets its span can fail a test, not just a dashboard.

docs.title: Parameter types
docs.text:
The type decides which validator runs over the value. It all lives in models/parameter.py: the ParamType enum and the VALIDATORS dictionary that maps each member to its function.

How to add a type

A new member in ParamType and a new entry in VALIDATORS. Nothing else. Do not scatter per-type if branches through the services — the dictionary exists precisely so validation stays in one place.

docs.title: The fifteen types
docs.text: Type Accepts Note string str int int float float or int int is accepted and preserved bool bool list list dict dict json str, dict or list A string is parsed; what gets stored is the object pattern str that compiles as a regex Validated with re.compile reference list[str] Each item must exist in referenced_params date str as YYYY-MM-DD datetime str as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS time str in ISO time format Validated with time.fromisoformat secret str or envelope Encrypted on write user dict with a fixed shape Encrypted on write users list of user Encrypted on write

docs.title: json converts
docs.text: If you send a string, what gets stored is the parsed object, not the string. Reading it back returns a dict or a list. An invalid string is a validation error.

docs.title: pattern only validates that it compiles
docs.text: The validator checks that the regex compiles — not that it matches anything. A syntactically valid, semantically wrong regex passes.

docs.title: reference needs the list alongside
docs.text:
The reference validator does not query the database: it checks against the referenced_params field of the parameter itself. Sending reference without referenced_params makes every reference fail, because the set of allowed names is empty.

{
  "DEPENDENCIES": {
    "value": ["TIMEOUT_HTTP", "BASE_URL"],
    "type": "reference",
    "referenced_params": ["TIMEOUT_HTTP", "BASE_URL", "RETRIES"]
  }
}

docs.title: user has a mandatory shape
docs.text:
Four fields, all required, with checked types:

Field Type user_id str user str password dict or str status bool

password accepting a dict is not sloppiness: it is the encrypted envelope coming back on a round trip. The client reads the parameter, receives password already as an envelope, and hands the envelope back on rewrite. Rejecting dict would break that round trip.

users is a list of user, and every item goes through the same validator.

docs.title: secret accepts both sides of the round trip
docs.text: str is the plaintext going in. dict is the envelope coming back — and in that case the validator checks that salt, master_key and crypto_data are all present, naming whichever are missing. Anything else is rejected.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Every parameter carries four bounds, and they have defaults:

Field Default Applies to min_length 0 str and list max_length 30 str and list min_value 0 int and float max_value 1000000 int and float

Two defaults that reject legitimate values nobody asked them to

max_length is 30. A connection string, a long URL or a token clears that easily and gets rejected with "Tamanho máximo excedido (30)".

min_value is 0. Any negative number is rejected with "Valor mínimo não atingido (0)".

In both cases the message is clear, but the cause does not look like a default — it looks like a bug. When storing a long string or a negative number, send the bounds explicitly.

Length checks run over str and list — which includes a reference's list and the result of a json that turned into a list.

docs.title: Validation order
docs.text:
1. The type validator runs first and may replace the value (that is the case for json, which swaps the string for the object).
  2. Then the length bounds, over the already converted value.
  3. Finally the numeric bounds.

The consequence: a json arriving as a string that becomes a 40-item list is blocked by the max_length of 30, even though the original string passed.

docs.title: Client overview
docs.text:
param-manager is the Python library that consumes the API. It is published on PyPI at version 0.4.3 and installed inside your application.

from param_manager import ParamManager

pm = ParamManager.get_instance()
timeout = pm.get_param('MY_APP', 'TIMEOUT_HTTP')

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
Reading configuration from a remote service adds a new dependency to your application's critical path. The library exists so that dependency degrades instead of failing:

  • Two-level cache, so most reads never touch the network.
  • Circuit breaker, to stop hammering a server that is sick.
  • Local TinyDB copy, which answers when the API does not.
  • Transparent decryption of sensitive parameters.

The price is that the value you read may be stale. How stale is your call — see Cache and offline mode.

docs.title: How a read is resolved
docs.text:
The chain below is walked until one step answers. The order is not accidental: each step costs more than the previous one, and the last one exists so that the absence of the API is degradation rather than failure.

flowchart TD
    accTitle: Resolution of a get_param in the client
    accDescr: A read tries the parameter cache first, then the application cache, then checks the circuit breaker, and only then goes to the network. Each check that succeeds returns the value through its own path; a network failure arms the breaker and falls back to the local TinyDB.

    A["ParamManager<br/>multiton by instance_name"] --> D1{"parameter cache<br/>still valid?"}

    D1 -- yes --> R1["return from the parameter cache"]
    D1 -- no --> D2{"application cache<br/>still valid?"}

    D2 -- yes --> R2["promote to the parameter cache<br/>and return the value"]
    D2 -- no --> D3{"breaker in cooldown?<br/>recent API error"}

    D3 -- yes --> R3["local TinyDB — offline mode<br/>params_<instance>.json"]
    D3 -- no --> B["GET /parameters/apps/.../params/...<br/>requests · timeout · verify_ssl<br/>optional auth headers"]

    B --> D4{"response 200 OK?"}

    D4 -- no --> R4["404, timeout, connection or 5xx<br/>arm the breaker and call<br/>_handle_api_error: TinyDB or None"]
    D4 -- yes --> R5["is it an envelope? decrypt<br/>AES-GCM + CHAVE_CUSTODIA_APP<br/>write cache and TinyDB, return"]

Writes have none of this. They always hit the network, always with a token, and never consult the cache:

flowchart LR
    accTitle: Write path in the client
    accDescr: The four write operations bypass the cache and TinyDB, require a token, and go straight to the API.

    W["create_app · upsert_params<br/>delete_param · delete_app"] --> T["_auth_headers<br/>token required"]
    T --> API["API"]
    W -. never consults .-x CACHE["cache · TinyDB"]

The detail of each step — cache validity, what arms and what disarms the breaker, and what happens in each failure mode — is in Cache and offline mode.

docs.title: Multiton, not singleton
docs.text:
ParamManager is not a singleton. It is a multiton: one instance per instance_name, held in a class dictionary guarded by a lock.

production = ParamManager.get_instance(instance_name='producao')
staging    = ParamManager.get_instance(instance_name='homolog')

The two have independent URLs, credentials, caches and local files.

The library's old documentation says 'Singleton'

The param-manager README and older pages on its site claim the class implements the Singleton pattern, with __instance and a one-hour cache. That describes a version that no longer exists. What holds is what is here.

__init__ returns early once an instance has been initialized, so constructing ParamManager(instance_name='x') twice returns the same object without redoing anything.

docs.title: The public surface
docs.text:
The package exports exactly two names:

from param_manager import ParamManager, ParamNaoEncontradoError

docs.title: Reading
docs.text: Method Returns get_param(app_name, param_name, save_cache=True) The value, already decrypted get_all_params(app_name) A name-to-value map

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
Method Note create_app(name, description=None) Expects 201 from the server upsert_params(app_name, param_name, *, value, param_type, ...) One parameter per call delete_param(app_name, param_name) delete_app(app_name)

Writes always hit the network, always with a token, and never consult the cache.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
Method Note clear_cache(app_name=None, param_name=None) With no argument, clears everything get_cache_info() Cache state, validity and error marks

Methods the old documentation promises and that do not exist

update_param(...) and get_param_schema(...) appear in the tutorial on the param-manager site. Neither exists. To change a value, use upsert_params.

docs.title: Python versions
docs.text:
requires-python = ">=3.10", with no ceiling. A pure library cannot know it will break on a version that does not exist yet, and the old ceiling, <=3.14, rejected even 3.14.1.

The floor moved from 3.8 to 3.10 for security, not syntax: python-dotenv==1.2.2 fixes PYSEC-2026-2270 and is not published below 3.10. On 3.9 the reachable ceiling is still vulnerable; on 3.8, worse. Lowering the floor means going back to shipping the flaw.

docs.title: The four steps
docs.text:
A call to get_param walks these, in order, until one of them answers:

  1. Parameter cache — keyed by app:param. The cheapest.
  2. Application cache — the whole map, filled by get_all_params. A hit here promotes the value into the parameter cache.
  3. Circuit breaker — if there is a recent error recorded for that application, the network is skipped and the answer comes from TinyDB.
  4. The network — a GET against the API. Success writes cache and TinyDB; failure arms the breaker and falls back to local.

get_all_params walks the same chain without step 2, which is itself.

docs.title: Cache validity
docs.text:
Governed by cache_duration, in seconds. The default depends on how the instance was created — 300 via the constructor, 3600 via get_instance.

There is no remote invalidation. A value changed on the server arrives when the cache expires, or when someone calls clear_cache. If you need fast propagation, what you tune is cache_duration — there is no push.

A negative CACHE_DURATION becomes 0, not the fallback. Zero means the cache is always invalid: every read goes to the network.

docs.title: What arms it
docs.text:
• Timeout
  • Connection error
  • A 404 handled as a missing parameter
  • Any unexpected error, including 5xx

That last item is worth highlighting: HTTP errors arm the cooldown alongside network errors. Without it, the library would hammer a server that is returning 500 on every read.

docs.title: How long it lasts
docs.text:
api_error_cooldown, in seconds. When unset, it falls back to cache_duration — which was the implicit value before the variable existed.

Why this variable was created

With get_instance, cache_duration is 3600. Before api_error_cooldown existed, a single transient 500 pinned the client to local data for an hour. If you use get_instance and care about fast recovery, set API_ERROR_COOLDOWN to something in the tens of seconds.

docs.title: What disarms it
docs.text:
• A successful request.
  • clear_cache for that application — unconditionally.

The two semantics are deliberately different: disarming on success is guarded by a compare-and-swap, disarming through clear_cache is not. Unifying them reintroduces an early-disarm race that has already been fixed.

docs.title: The local file
docs.text:
<base>/param_manager/<instance_name>/params_<instance_name>.json

One TinyDB per instance. Written on every successful read from the API; read when the network fails or the breaker is armed.

The local file is not a pre-warmed cache

It only contains what has been successfully read at least once. On a fresh machine, with the API down from the start, it is empty and get_param returns None. Offline mode survives an outage; it does not replace the first read.

docs.title: When a read fails
docs.text:
Every failure path converges on _handle_api_error, which tries TinyDB and returns whatever is there — or None.

Situation Result Parameter never read, API down None Parameter read before, API down The last known value Parameter deleted on the server 404, breaker armed, local value still returned Wrong custody key None, with an error in the log

That third row has a practical consequence: deleting a parameter on the server does not immediately remove it from clients that had already read it. They keep returning the local value while the breaker is armed.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
The library is used from multiple threads and its state is guarded by three distinct locks:

Lock Guards _lock_singleton The multiton instance dictionary _token_lock Token renewal — separate to avoid re-entrancy _state_lock Caches and error marks

Reads take a snapshot under the lock and process outside it, so the lock is not held during work that does not need it.

docs.title: A residual accepted on purpose
docs.text: The client's compare-and-swap resolves a timestamp tie in favour of writing. That is not an oversight: the cost asymmetry between writing again and losing a write favours writing. It is documented at the point in the code and should not be "fixed" on sight.

docs.title: The precedence order
docs.text:
For almost everything, the order is:

constructor argument  >  {INSTANCE_NAME}_VARIABLE  >  VARIABLE

The prefix is the instance_name in upper case. With instance_name='producao', the specific variable is PRODUCAO_CACHE_DURATION and the generic one is CACHE_DURATION.

Two variables invert that order

TIMEOUT and CACHE_DURATION do not follow the rule: today the environment variable beats the constructor argument. Passing timeout=30 in code has no effect if TIMEOUT exists in the environment.

This is known debt and it is recorded. Fixing it means changing the get_instance defaults to None, which alters a public signature — which is why it is held for a larger version.

docs.title: Connection
docs.text:
Variable Alternatives Default API_{INSTANCE}_URL API_PARAMS_URL, API_URL '' TIMEOUT — 5 VERIFY_SSL {INSTANCE}_VERIFY_SSL False

The URL is resolved in this order: the api_url argument, then API_{INSTANCE}_URL, then API_PARAMS_URL, then API_URL. There is no instance prefix on the last two.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Variable Default {INSTANCE}_PARAMS_USERNAME or PARAMS_USERNAME (none) {INSTANCE}_PARAMS_PASSWORD or PARAMS_PASSWORD (none)

The old tutorial gets the names wrong

The older documentation mentions PARAM_MANAGER_USERNAME and PARAM_MANAGER_PASSWORD. The correct names are PARAMS_USERNAME and PARAMS_PASSWORD.

docs.title: Cache and resilience
docs.text:
Variable Alternative Default CACHE_DURATION {INSTANCE}_CACHE_DURATION 300 via the constructor, 3600 via get_instance API_ERROR_COOLDOWN {INSTANCE}_API_ERROR_COOLDOWN Falls back to cache_duration

The cache default depends on how you construct

ParamManager(...) uses 300 s. ParamManager.get_instance(...) uses 3600 s. Both forms are public and both values are in the code. If cache validity matters to you, pass the value explicitly.

docs.title: Local storage
docs.text:
Variable Default LOCAL_DB_PATH The .env directory, or the current directory

The final file lands at:

<base>/param_manager/<instance_name>/params_<instance_name>.json

The base is resolved in this order: the local_db_path argument, then the PyInstaller directory when frozen, then LOCAL_DB_PATH, then the .env directory, and finally the working directory.

The path changed in 0.4.0

The old documentation mentions param_manager/params_db.json, without the instance level. Since 0.4.0 there is one directory per instance.

docs.title: Cryptography
docs.text:
Variable Alternative CHAVE_CUSTODIA_APP APP_CUSTODY_KEY

It must match the server's APP_CUSTODY_KEY. If it does not, decryption fails — and it fails silently: the client logs an error and returns None. See Cryptographic envelope.

docs.title: Legacy cache
docs.text:
Variable Effect PARAM_MANAGER_PURGE_PLAINTEXT_CACHE Purges, at startup, old local cache written in the clear

It is opt-in. Turn it on once when migrating from a version that stored sensitive values unencrypted.

docs.title: verify_ssl has partial scope
docs.text:
This is the easiest thing in the whole library to misdiagnose.

The flag governs only the two read GETs. Authentication and writes always verify the TLS chain, and that is deliberate: POST /auth/token carries a username and password, and weakening its TLS would be worse than the asymmetry.

The symptom in an environment with an internal certificate

Reads work and authentication fails with an SSL error. It looks like half-finished configuration; it is the designed behaviour. The right fix is to install the internal chain on the system, not to hunt for a flag that disables verification on login.

verify_ssl defaults to False, because the environments consuming this library use internal certificates. Anyone with a trusted chain can — and should — pass verify_ssl=True.

The values accepted in the environment variable are 1, true, yes and on, case-insensitively. Anything else is false.

docs.title: Sample .env
docs.text:
API_PARAMS_URL=https://parameters.example.com
PARAMS_USERNAME=reporting-service
PARAMS_PASSWORD=...
CACHE_DURATION=600
API_ERROR_COOLDOWN=60
VERIFY_SSL=true
CHAVE_CUSTODIA_APP=...

# A second instance, with its own overrides
API_HOMOLOG_URL=https://parameters-staging.example.com
HOMOLOG_CACHE_DURATION=30

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text: The library has explicit PyInstaller support. That matters because two things it does — reading a .env and writing a local file — change location once the application becomes an executable.

docs.title: How it detects being frozen
docs.text:
if getattr(sys, 'frozen', False):
    base_dir = sys._MEIPASS
    dotenv_path = os.path.join(base_dir, '.env')
else:
    base_dir = None
    dotenv_path = find_dotenv()

sys.frozen is the marker PyInstaller leaves; sys._MEIPASS is the temporary directory it extracts resources into.

docs.title: Consequence for .env
docs.text:
Once frozen, the library looks for .env inside the bundle, not next to the executable. It has to be embedded:

pyinstaller --onefile --add-data ".env;." my_app.py

On Linux and macOS the separator is : instead of ;.

An embedded .env travels with the binary

Any secret inside it ships in the executable and can be extracted by whoever has it. For real credentials, prefer system environment variables — which are still read normally — over embedding.

docs.title: Consequence for the local file
docs.text:
When frozen and without an explicit local_db_path, the TinyDB base becomes sys._MEIPASS.

sys._MEIPASS is deleted when the process exits

Under --onefile, that directory is temporary. The local file is created, used, and disappears at the end of the run — and with it the whole offline mode: the next run starts with no survival copy at all.

Pass a persistent path:

import os

pm = ParamManager.get_instance(
    local_db_path=os.path.join(
        os.environ['LOCALAPPDATA'], 'MyApp'
    )
)

Or set LOCAL_DB_PATH in the environment. The resolution order gives the argument precedence over the frozen directory.

Under --onedir the directory survives between runs, but it still sits inside the installation folder — which is usually inappropriate in a write-protected directory. The explicit-path recommendation holds in both modes.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• .env embedded with --add-data, or configuration coming from the environment
  • local_db_path or LOCAL_DB_PATH pointing at a persistent, writable directory
  • CHAVE_CUSTODIA_APP available at runtime, if there is any sensitive parameter
  • The environment's certificate chain installed, if verify_ssl=True — or awareness that authentication always verifies TLS, even with verify_ssl=False (see Configuration)

docs.title: Why the library is a single module
docs.text: param_manager/manager.py holds everything. That is deliberate: every extra file is another chance for the packager not to find something, and dynamic imports are exactly what PyInstaller's static analysers cannot see.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install param-manager Successfully installed param-manager-0.4.3

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer. The floor is a security decision — see Client overview.
  • Network access to the API, at least for the first read of each parameter. Without one successful read there is nothing to fall back to: the local file starts empty.

docs.title: What comes with it
docs.text: Dependency For what requests The HTTP calls tinydb The local survival copy pycryptodome Decryption of sensitive parameters python-dotenv Reading .env

docs.title: Verifying
docs.text:
import param_manager

print(param_manager.__version__)   # 0.4.3

docs.title: Development environment
docs.text:
For anyone working on the library itself:

cd param-manager
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

Commands:

task test              # runs `task fix` first, then pytest with coverage
task test_unit         # unit only
task test_integracao   # only what writes to a real TinyDB
task lint
task format

task test rewrites your code before testing

param-manager's pre_test is task fix, which runs ruff check . --fix. That is: the source is modified before the suite runs. Review the diff before calling the task done — changes you did not write may have come along.

Install ruff at the pinned version

ruff==0.11.7 in this project. Newer versions bring preview rules that flag violations the code does not have — a false positive that has already cost a wrong diagnosis.

docs.title: Why the integration suite exists
docs.text:
Because the mocks lie, in specific and known places. The most expensive one: a mocked table.get() returns the same object on every call — an aliasing the real TinyDB does not have, and which has already hidden a persistence bug with the whole suite green.

When you do need a mock anyway:

mock_table.get.side_effect = lambda *a, **k: copy.deepcopy(...)

Concurrency tests use an injected barrier or a side_effect that mutates state mid-iteration — never sleep and hope. faulthandler_timeout = 60 is configured, so a test that hangs dumps every thread's stack instead of pinning the runner.

docs.title: Getting an instance
docs.text:
from param_manager import ParamManager

pm = ParamManager.get_instance()

With explicit configuration:

pm = ParamManager.get_instance(
    instance_name='producao',
    api_url='https://parameters.example.com',
    cache_duration=600,
    timeout=10,
    verify_ssl=True,
    api_error_cooldown=60,
)

The full constructor signature:

ParamManager(
    api_url: str | None = None,
    cache_duration: int = 300,
    timeout: int = 5,
    local_db_path: str | None = None,
    username: str | None = None,
    password: str | None = None,
    instance_name: str = 'default',
    verify_ssl: bool | None = None,
    api_error_cooldown: int | None = None,
)

get_instance takes the same arguments, but with cache_duration=3600 — see Configuration.

docs.title: One parameter
docs.text:
timeout = pm.get_param('MY_APP', 'TIMEOUT_HTTP')

Returns the value ready to use: converted by its type and, if sensitive, already decrypted. The caller never sees an envelope.

The third argument, save_cache, controls whether the result feeds the cache. Use save_cache=False for a one-off read that should not influence the next ones.

Absence returns None, not an exception

When the parameter does not exist, when the API is down and there is no local copy, or when decryption fails, get_param returns None. All three are indistinguishable in the return value — the difference only shows up in the log.

If None is a legitimate value in your domain, you cannot tell them apart. Use your own sentinel:

MISSING = object()
value = pm.get_param('MY_APP', 'X')
if value is None:
    value = MISSING

docs.title: All at once
docs.text:
params = pm.get_all_params('MY_APP')

Returns a name-to-value dictionary. Besides being a single request, this fills the application cache, and subsequent individual reads hit it without touching the network.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text: Every write hits the network, requires a token and ignores the cache.

docs.title: Create an application
docs.text:
pm.create_app('MY_APP', 'Reporting service')

Expects 201 from the server. Any other status raises.

docs.title: Write a parameter
docs.text:
pm.upsert_params(
    'MY_APP',
    'TIMEOUT_HTTP',
    value=30,
    param_type='int',
    description='Timeout for outbound calls',
    max_value=300,
)

Signature:

upsert_params(
    app_name: str,
    param_name: str,
    *,
    value: Any,
    param_type: str,
    description: str | None = None,
    user_editable: bool | None = None,
    min_length: int | None = None,
    max_length: int | None = None,
    min_value: int | float | None = None,
    max_value: int | float | None = None,
    referenced_params: list[str] | None = None,
)

Everything after app_name and param_name is keyword-only.

user_editable=None is different from False

The default is None, and in that case the key is omitted from the payload. That is what lets the server tell "I did not send it" from "I sent False" — the distinction that editing a user_editable parameter as a plain user depends on under USER_EDITABLE_ENFORCEMENT=explicit.

Version 0.4.2 sent False explicitly. If you assemble the payload by hand, do not reintroduce that.

Remember the bounds: max_length is 30 on the server by default. To store a long string, pass max_length explicitly — see Parameter types.

docs.title: Store a secret
docs.text:
pm.upsert_params(
    'MY_APP',
    'DB_PASSWORD',
    value='r3al-p4ssw0rd',
    param_type='secret',
    max_length=200,
)

The value travels in the clear over the connection (which is why HTTPS matters) and is encrypted by the server before it touches the database. Reading it back, decryption is transparent.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
pm.delete_param('MY_APP', 'TIMEOUT_HTTP')
pm.delete_app('MY_APP')

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
pm.clear_cache('MY_APP', 'TIMEOUT_HTTP')  # one parameter
pm.clear_cache('MY_APP')                  # the whole application
pm.clear_cache()                          # everything

clear_cache also disarms the circuit breaker

Clearing an application's cache drops its error mark unconditionally. It is an explicit operator action: it means "try again now" after fixing the API, without waiting for the cooldown.

info = pm.get_cache_info()

Returns the cached applications, the timestamps, whether each entry is still valid, and the per-application error marks.

docs.title: Multiple instances
docs.text:
production = ParamManager.get_instance(
    instance_name='producao', api_url='https://parameters.example.com'
)
staging = ParamManager.get_instance(
    instance_name='homolog', api_url='https://parameters-staging.example.com'
)

Each has its own cache, credentials and local file. Nothing leaks from one to the other.

docs.title: In your tests
docs.text:
The multiton holds instances in a class dictionary that survives between tests. Without resetting it, one test reuses the instance another one created:

def setup_function():
    ParamManager._instances = {}

Without this, a test that configures a different api_url will silently use the previous test's URL.

docs.text:
Who talks to whom, across the whole product:

The two artifacts are released separately, and whatever crosses the arrow between them is contract — see Compatibility.

docs.title: The server layers
docs.text:
The server is strictly layered, and one rule holds everything together: a controller never touches the database. The full flowchart of a request, with Keycloak, cryptography and telemetry alongside, is in API overview.

Each layer owns something the others are not licensed to take over:

controllers/ Translates HTTP into a business call. Declares dependencies through Depends — this is where the decision of who may call what lives. It does not know MongoDB exists. services/ The rules. AppService validates permission, encrypts sensitive values and assembles metadata. RuntimeConfigService resolves configuration that can change without a redeploy. repositories/ The only place that talks to Mongo. This is where the conditional write that guards against concurrent updates lives. models/ and schemas/ models/ holds the domain model and, most importantly, the VALIDATORS dictionary that defines what each parameter type accepts. schemas/ holds the API's request and response contracts.

docs.title: Dependency injection is a test contract
docs.text: The controller module exposes the get_app_service factory and re-exports get_current_user and require_admin. The test suite overrides exactly those names through app.dependency_overrides. Changing how they are imported breaks the tests without breaking the application — the worst possible order in which to find out about a problem.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text: Concurrent state on the server is versioned by AppModel.params_version, a counter. Never by updated_at. The two used to be the same field, and while they were, any date normalization on the audit side turned every write into a conflict — with a diffuse symptom and no failing test.

docs.title: Read resolution in the client
docs.text:
The full flowchart, with all four steps and every exit, is in Client overview.

The order is not accidental. Each step costs more than the previous one, and the last one — TinyDB — exists so that the absence of the API is degradation rather than failure.

Writes have none of this: create_app, upsert_params, delete_param and delete_app always hit the network, always with a token, and never consult the cache.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
This is the most important page on the site for anyone about to change something.

The client and the API are published separately. The client lives on PyPI, is installed by third parties and updated whenever they feel like it — possibly never. The server never asks who it is talking to. From that follows one rule with three faces, and satisfying one is not satisfying the rule.

docs.title: 1. The HTTP contract
docs.text:
Nothing may:

  • reject a payload that is accepted today;
  • change the shape of a success response;
  • introduce a new status code on an existing route;
  • drop a metric label that some dashboard consumes;
  • change the security scheme published in the OpenAPI document.

docs.title: 2. Clients already in production
docs.text:
The client compares the status exactly:

if res.status_code != HTTPStatus.OK:
    raise Exception(...)

That has a consequence which usually catches people by surprise: returning 201 where 200 used to come back breaks the fleet, even though 201 is "more correct". A success change is still a break.

The practical corollary

No response change is safe merely because the semantics improved. The right question is not "is this response more correct?" but "can a client of any already-published version tell the difference?".

docs.title: 3. Data already stored
docs.text:
A parameter already saved must keep decrypting and keep being writable.

  • The cryptographic envelope is a frozen contract between two artifacts released on different dates — see Cryptographic envelope.
  • A document written before a new field existed must not start erroring. In Mongo a filter on null matches a missing field, and that is what makes lazy migration possible, with no migration script.

docs.title: What is not contract
docs.text: A path that today ends in an unhandled exception or a silent failure is not contract. Nobody can depend on a process that dies. Fixing a crash does not break compatibility, even if it changes what the client observes.

docs.title: None of this is enforced by CI
docs.text:
Worth saying plainly: no automated test guarantees anything on this page.

What exists is tests/test_openapi_contrato.py, which freezes only securitySchemes and the per-route security block. It does not freeze the routes themselves, nor the methods, nor the success statuses, nor the response shapes. And no job crosses the two repositories.

The rule is held up by review, not by a test. It matters most right before a coordinated release of both sides.

docs.title: Release order
docs.text:
When a change has to happen on both sides, the order is always the same:

  1. Server first, inert. Every observable behaviour change goes behind a setting whose default reproduces the current state. The new server behaves exactly like the old one.
  2. Client next. Published to PyPI, adopted at the pace of whoever consumes it.
  3. The switch last, once telemetry shows there are no old clients left — and only then.

Two real examples of this pattern are documented: READ_AUTH_MODE and USER_EDITABLE_ENFORCEMENT. In both cases the default is the historical behaviour, and promotion depends on a measurement, not on a date.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The terms below have a precise meaning in this product. Where common usage differs, that is stated.

Application (app) The grouping unit for parameters. In MongoDB it is a document; in the API it is everything after /parameters/apps/. Identified by its name, which is unique. Unrelated to "application" in the sense of a running process — several processes can read the same application. Parameter A named entry inside an application. It has a value, a type and a set of metadata: description, user_editable, length and value bounds, and the list of allowed references. Parameter type (ParamType) One of the fifteen enum values that decides which validator runs over the value. See Parameter types. Envelope The structure a sensitive value is stored in: salt, master_key and crypto_data. It never contains the plaintext. See Cryptographic envelope. Custody key The application secret from which the key protecting the master_key is derived. On the server it comes from APP_CUSTODY_KEY; on the client, from CHAVE_CUSTODIA_APP or APP_CUSTODY_KEY. Multiton The ParamManager pattern: not a single global instance, but one instance per instance_name. Two instances with different names have independent configuration, cache and local file. The library's older documentation calls this a singleton — it is wrong. Instance (instance_name) The name identifying one client configuration. It acts as the multiton key, as the environment variable prefix, and as the directory and file name of the TinyDB. Parameter cache Fine-grained cache, keyed by app:param. The first step of read resolution. Application cache Cache of an application's entire parameter map, filled by get_all_params. The second step: a hit here promotes the value into the parameter cache. Circuit breaker (cooldown) The window during which the client stops trying the network after an error. Armed by timeout, connection error, a handled 404, or any unexpected failure; disarmed by a successful request or by an explicit clear_cache. Local fallback Reading from TinyDB when the API is unavailable. It only returns what has been successfully read at least once. params_version A per-application counter used to detect concurrent writes on the server. It is not version history and does not allow returning to a previous state. READ_AUTH_MODE Runtime setting that decides whether reading a parameter requires a token: off, warn or enforce. See Authentication. user_editable A flag on a parameter authorizing a plain user to change only the value field. Any metadata change still requires an admin. integracao marker A pytest marker for whatever talks to a real resource — a real Mongo on the server, a real TinyDB file on the client. It exists because the mocks lie in specific, documented places.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Configuration scattered across a .env file per machine has three defects that only show up once the system grows: nobody knows the current value in production, changing a value requires a deploy, and plaintext passwords end up in backups, in logs and in git history.

Centralizing it in a service fixes all three — and creates a fourth: now the application won't start if the configuration service is down. Param Manager is designed around that trade. The client never depends on the API being up at the moment it reads.

docs.title: The two artifacts
docs.text:
fast-param-manager param-manager What it is HTTP API Python library Where it runs A server, in a container Inside your application Distribution Image / your own deploy PyPI — pip install param-manager Stores in MongoDB Local TinyDB, as a survival copy Version 2.0.0 0.4.3

They are versioned and released independently. There is no atomic deploy of both: there is always a window where an old client talks to a new server. That is the constraint that shapes the product the most, and it has its own page — Compatibility.

There is also a planned third directory, front-param-manager, currently empty. Not a line of code exists, and nothing in this documentation depends on it.

docs.title: What the API does
docs.text:
• Stores parameters grouped by application. An application is a document in Mongo; the parameters are a map inside it.
  • Validates each value against its type. Fifteen types, from string to users, each with its own validator — including a compilable regex, a date in a fixed format, and a reference to another parameter that must exist.
  • Encrypts what is sensitive. Types secret, user and users are never written in the clear.
  • Decides who writes what. An admin does everything; a plain user only changes the value field of parameters flagged as editable.
  • Reports on itself. Every controller, service and repository opens an OpenTelemetry span and records metrics.

docs.title: What the client does
docs.text:
• Resolves a parameter cheapest-path-first: parameter cache, application cache, and only then the network.
  • Stops hammering a sick server. A network or HTTP error arms a circuit breaker with a configurable window.
  • Survives the API being down. Every parameter successfully read is written to a local TinyDB, which becomes the source when the network fails.
  • Decrypts secrets with the application custody key, without the caller needing to know encryption was involved.
  • Isolates instances. ParamManager is a multiton: one instance per name, each with its own configuration, cache and local file.

docs.title: What the product deliberately does not do
docs.text:
Worth knowing what not to look for here:

  • It does not negotiate client versions. The server does not know who it is talking to and does not change behaviour because of it.
  • It does not push changes in real time. There is no push, no websocket, no remote cache invalidation. A changed value reaches a client when that client's cache expires.
  • It does not protect reads by default. Out of the box, reading a parameter is anonymous. That is configurable at runtime, and the authentication page explains why the default is what it is and how to move away from it safely.
  • It does not version a parameter's value. There is a version counter per application, used to detect concurrent writes — it is not history, and there is no rolling back.

docs.title: Cryptographic envelope
docs.text:
Parameters of type secret, user and users are never stored in the clear. They are kept in a two-layer envelope.

This format is a frozen contract

The server encrypts in security/crypto_utils.py; the client decrypts in ParamManager._descriptografar_param. These are two duplicated implementations, in repositories released on different dates.

Changing one side alone fails silently: the client merely logs an error and returns None. There is no exception, no alarm, and the value simply becomes None in the consuming application.

docs.title: The format
docs.text:
{
  "salt": "<hex>",
  "master_key":  { "iv": "<hex>", "tag": "<hex>", "data": "<hex>" },
  "crypto_data": { "iv": "<hex>", "tag": "<hex>", "data": "<hex>" }
}

Two layers:

  1. A custody key, derived from the application secret, protects the master_key.
  2. The master_key protects the real data, in crypto_data.

docs.title: The frozen parameters
docs.text:
Changing any of these invalidates every secret already stored and every client already published to PyPI:

Item Value Derivation PBKDF2(custody_key, salt, dkLen=32, count=100_000, hmac_hash_module=SHA256) Cipher AES-GCM IV 12 bytes, random Authentication The GCM tag Serialization Everything hex

docs.title: The custody key
docs.text:
Side Variable Default Server APP_CUSTODY_KEY, through settings dev-chave-custodia-app Client CHAVE_CUSTODIA_APP or APP_CUSTODY_KEY (none)

The development default is not a secret

dev-chave-custodia-app is in public source code. An environment brought up without changing APP_CUSTODY_KEY has its secrets encrypted with a key anyone knows — which is equivalent to not encrypting them.

docs.title: The legacy tolerance
docs.text:
The client's parser accepts the key dado as a synonym for data, inherited from an earlier format.

Keep that fallback when touching the parser. Removing it breaks any value written before the rename, which is still in the database and has no migration.

docs.title: The round trip
docs.text:
The envelope comes back to the server whenever a client reads and rewrites a parameter. That is why the validators accept both forms:

  • secret accepts a str (plaintext going in) or a dict (the envelope coming back). For the dict case it checks that salt, master_key and crypto_data are all present.
  • On the user type, the password field accepts str or dict for the same reason.

Rejecting the dict would look stricter and would break the round trip.

docs.title: Where TLS comes in
docs.text:
The plaintext travels over the network on write: the server is what encrypts, not the client. Without HTTPS the secret is exposed in transit, and the envelope only protects what is at rest in the database.

Add to that the client's partial verify_ssl scope — which governs reads only — and the practical conclusion is one: use HTTPS with a valid chain. See Client configuration.

docs.title: Known and deliberate limitation
docs.text:
In the users branch of AppService._encrypt_value, a single salt and a single master_key serve every user in the parameter, and the same encrypted_master_key dictionary is aliased into all the envelopes.

This is known and out of scope by explicit decision: there is an in-progress design for finer granularity, with one master key per parameter. Do not "fix" it piecemeal — the change has to be designed as a whole, together with the migration of data already stored.

docs.title: Audit already applied
docs.text: The security/crypto_utils.py module went through a dedicated review and the findings were applied: the module-level salt, the config.json that was written to the working directory, and the dead store_credentials / recover_password pair that used them are all gone.

docs.title: If decryption fails
docs.text:
The symptom is always the same — None instead of the value, and an error in the log. The likely causes, in order:

  1. A different custody key between client and server.
  2. An incomplete envelope, from a write made by hand outside the API.
  3. Client and server versions with divergent envelope implementations — which only happens if the contract was changed on one side alone.

Start with the first: it is by far the most common.
